groups.title: Normal Forms & Anomalies
groups.question: Explain what normalization is and why we bother with it.

followUps.1NF Through 3NF — What They Actually Pre: Pick one normal form and describe the data problem it prevents.
followUps.BCNF & When to Stop Normalizing: When would you choose to denormalize, and what risk do you take on when you do?

evidence.text: Normalization stores each fact once, so it can't be updated in one place and left stale in another.
Names a concrete anomaly a normal form prevents, e.g. a customer's address repeated on every order and updated on only some.
Each column should depend on the whole key and nothing but the key.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says normalization exists to make queries faster.

evidence.text: Denormalize when a read-heavy workload pays too much for joins, and you've measured it.
The cost is duplicated data that can get out of sync, so every write must update all copies.
It should be a documented, deliberate trade-off.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (BCNF, denormalization) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

groups.title: ER Diagrams & Constraints
groups.question: Walk through how you turn business requirements into a schema that protects its own data.

followUps.Entity-Relationship Modeling: What can go wrong if you skip the ER diagram and guess the relationships between tables?
followUps.CHECK, UNIQUE & NOT NULL Constraints: Why put a rule in a database constraint when the application already validates it?

evidence.text: An ER diagram makes you decide each relationship's cardinality (one-to-many, many-to-many) before building tables.
Guessing wrong, like modelling many-to-many as one-to-many, loses or duplicates data from day one.
Many-to-many relationships need a join table.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (ER diagram, entity, relationship) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says the ER diagram is only documentation with no effect on the schema.

evidence.text: Constraints are enforced by the database on every write, whoever does it.
Application checks can be bypassed by another service, a manual fix, a script or a buggy deploy.
NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK express rules like required, no duplicates, or a valid range.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (CHECK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says validation in the application is enough.

groups.title: Keys & Relationships
groups.question: Explain how you choose keys and link tables together.

followUps.Surrogate vs Natural Keys: What problem does a surrogate key solve, and what extra constraint does it still need?
followUps.Cascading Actions & Referential Integrit: When is ON DELETE CASCADE the right choice, and when could it cause serious data loss?

evidence.text: Natural keys like an email can change, and then every referencing row has to change too.
A surrogate key (generated id) never changes, so references stay stable.
The natural value still needs its own UNIQUE constraint to stop duplicates.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (surrogate key, natural key) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a surrogate key alone stops duplicate records.

evidence.text: ON DELETE CASCADE deletes the child rows automatically when the parent is deleted.
That's right when children can't exist without the parent, like order lines of an order.
On important or shared data it can silently wipe out large trees of rows.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (ON DELETE CASCADE, RESTRICT) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says CASCADE should be the default for every foreign key.

groups.title: Schema Migration Strategy
groups.question: Walk through how a team should change a database schema over time without breaking things.

followUps.Versioned Migrations with Tools: What goes wrong when a team runs schema SQL scripts by hand, and how do migration tools prevent it?
followUps.Zero-Downtime Schema Changes: How would you rename or replace a column on a large, busy table without downtime?

evidence.text: Running scripts by hand means nobody knows what ran where, so environments drift apart.
A migration tool records which numbered migrations ran, in order, and applies only the missing ones.
Every environment gets the same schema the same way, and changes are reviewed in git.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (Flyway, Liquibase, migrations) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says migration tools automatically undo any bad change.

evidence.text: Many ALTER TABLE changes take a lock that blocks reads and writes on a busy table.
Add the new column, write to both, backfill in batches, switch reads, then drop the old one.
Each step is small and backwards compatible, so the app keeps running throughout.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (ALTER TABLE, expand/contract) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says renaming a column in place is always safe on a busy table.
